M01: I left both drive torques at zero for two seconds. The axle stayed at its starting point in Python and drifted by at most 0.0632 mm in Simscape.
M02: In the Gazebo run shown here, the robot entered the stop band 63 ms after the brake command. The Simscape run took 471 ms with its own command profile.
M03: On the 0.40 m Simscape arc, radial RMSE was 1.90 mm. The caster ended at −31.36°.
M04: The robot followed two opposing arcs. Cross-track RMSE was 12.62 mm in Python and 1.15 mm in the Simscape continuous-arc check. Each controller used its own speed profile.
M05: Both models completed all four edges and four turns. The Python run finished at 32.50 s, 7.26 mm from the target.
M06: Both models completed the eight steps in the reverse direction. Simscape confirmed the final stop at 60.07 s.
M07: The first route touched a wall in Gazebo. I revised the route with 60 mm corners, which left 23.38 mm of minimum clearance for the shared robot envelope.
M08: I started the caster at +30° and −30°. Both runs met the settling criterion once I extended the reverse segment. The original segment was too short.
M09: Pivot from a 90° or 180° caster start
The Simscape sequence passed at both settings when it included a short launch. The best separate 180° pivot with zero forward request ended 26.78 mm from its start. The limit was 20 mm.
M10: In Simscape, the run with 5 kg on the robot finished 7.81 mm from the target. The nominal run finished 12.00 mm away.
M11: The Gazebo drive wheels crossed the boundary at 2.035 s. The caster reached it at 3.568 s. Braking distance in that run was 16.63 mm.
M12: The models crossed different 5 mm fixtures. Simscape cleared a beveled trim and Gazebo cleared a threshold. The sharp Simscape fixture and the 20 mm Gazebo trial stalled.
Q01: The Python controller held the tag at the target for 0.40 s before asking the robot to move forward. Simscape held its optical depth and position targets at the same time.
Q02: Both controllers turned left toward the tag. Final position error was 1.27 mm in Python and 14.00 mm in the Simscape fixture.
Q03: Both controllers turned right. The Python run ended 1.27 mm from the target, the same as the mirrored run with the tag on the left.
Q04: The Gazebo robot stopped with the tag centered and the axle 43.70 mm from the nominal docking pose. In the second run I used all four corners and added a positioning maneuver. I also changed the optical stop target from 265 to 260 mm. The final error was 6.236 mm.
Q05: The Gazebo robot found the tag 2.454 s into the search. The controller kept its forward command at zero while it looked.
Q06: Both controllers cut the forward command when the first invalid observation arrived. Simscape confirmed a stop at 1.417 s and latched an abort at 2.060 s.
Q07: I moved the tag 120 mm to the side before putting it back in view. Gazebo held the new center for 0.406 s before requesting forward motion.
Q08: The live Gazebo camera read the wrong station tag 47 times. The search ended after 3.200 s with zero forward requests and zero success events.
Q09: The Linux camera replay contained 12 frames with two copies of the target ID. The controller treated them as ambiguous and the simulated robot stopped.
Q10: I used modified Gazebo camera frames to test three disturbances. The longest distance to a confirmed stop was 3.843 mm.
Q11: The controller rejected stale frames during the camera replay. The pose log shows the simulated robot stopping after the observation became invalid.
Q12: Covering the tag or losing its corners made the observation invalid. The forward command and the simulated speed reached zero.
Q13: In live ROS 2, the command went to zero when the latest camera data was 203 ms old. Separate checks caught repeated and backward timestamps.
Q14: Gazebo entered the stop band in 40 ms after traveling 2.681 mm. The robot moved again once the corridor was clear, an operator authorized it and a fresh tag was visible.
Q15: The Gazebo robot reached a 2.66 mm pose error and registered simulated contact. The controller kept waiting for charging confirmation, then timed out.
Q16: After contact, Gazebo accepted the virtual BMS message once it was fresh and the robot was stationary.
Q17: The third QR loss used up the two retries. After the abort, the Gazebo controller issued no further motion command.
Q18: The Gazebo robot waited for the virtual charging disconnect, then reversed 0.577 m. Minimum clearance was 81.7 mm.
Q19: Gazebo met the optical criterion with the rotated tag. A separate pose measurement showed 31.82 mm of position error and 3.41° of yaw error.
Q20: In the Python delay test, damping cut yaw sign changes from 23 to two. Both Simscape variants recorded four.
O01: Gazebo used a separate goal ID for each stop on the A to B to A route. The robot stopped 7.51 mm from the target at B.
O02: Turn and back out of a narrow corridor
Gazebo reversed out with zero wall contacts. The closest clearance for the shared robot envelope was 10.91 mm.
O03: A moving test block represents the crossing. Gazebo stopped in 67 ms after moving 6.081 mm. When I withheld restart permission in a separate run, it stayed stopped.
O04: In Gazebo, the controller detected the command interruption at 246 ms. The robot entered the stop band 41 ms later. The cancellation test blocked later positive motion requests.
O05: In ROS 2, the guard rejected 18 unauthorized requests. Permission arrived at 1.983 s. The robot moved at 2.340 s after receiving a new command.
O06: I added a 4 kg payload. The robot parked 4.264 mm from the target in Python and 7.57 mm away in Gazebo.
O07: Return to dock at low battery
At a simulated 12% charge, Gazebo stopped its current task before starting the docking sequence. A fresh virtual BMS confirmation finished the run.
O08: Recovery after power or connection returns
Once the clock returned, all 30 unauthorized requests got zero output from the guard. Motion started after authorization and a fresh command.
